items.title: DeepMind launches Genie 4 world model enabling unprecedented realism in real-time simulation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Genie 4: A new generation of world simulation
items.summary:
DeepMind has introduced Genie 4, a new generation world model designed to enhance realism in real-time simulations. This advancement represents a significant step forward in the development of AI-driven world simulation technologies.

Genie 4 builds on previous models to provide more detailed and accurate representations of complex environments, potentially benefiting applications in gaming, robotics, and virtual reality. The model aims to unlock new possibilities for interactive and dynamic simulations by improving the fidelity and responsiveness of virtual worlds.

items.title: Survival LLM launches offline AI assistant and emergency library with trusted sources for Mac and Windows [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Survival LLM: AI assistant and emergency library that runs on your own computer
items.summary:
Survival LLM is a free, open-source AI assistant that runs entirely on a user's computer without internet access, providing emergency information on topics like food safety, first aid, and water purification. It sources answers from a comprehensive library including medical references, government guides, survival manuals, and about 930,000 Wikipedia articles, showing exact source passages for verification.

The app adapts to available computer memory by downloading an appropriately sized AI model and requires an initial setup with internet to download the model and library, which can take from 20 minutes to over two hours. It supports adding personal documents for search and maintains privacy by not sending queries online. The software runs on Apple Silicon Macs with macOS 14 or newer and 64-bit Windows 10 or 11, requiring significant disk space for installation.

items.title: Raspberry Pi Zero 3 W and Pi 4 Model A device trees appear in Linux kernel, revealing new board details
items.originalTitle: Raspberry Pi Zero 3W and Pi 4 Model A spotted in device trees
items.summary:
Device tree files for the Raspberry Pi Zero 3 W and Raspberry Pi 4 Model A have been added to the Raspberry Pi Linux kernel source, indicating upcoming new models without official announcements. The Zero 3 W appears to use the Broadcom BCM2711 SoC from the Pi 4, suggesting a significant performance upgrade, while the Pi 4 Model A resembles a stripped-down Pi 4 Model B with fewer ports and no Ethernet.

The Zero 3 W device tree hints at features like a single HDMI output, a power button, and possibly eMMC storage, though some details may be placeholders. The Pi 4 Model A lacks Ethernet and analog audio but may support an external antenna, similar to the Compute Module 4. Both boards include SPI flash bootloaders and maintain compatibility with existing GPIO layouts. These findings come from analysis of the device trees and have yet to be confirmed by official Raspberry Pi announcements.

items.title: Researchers formalize the classification of finite simple groups in Lean, uncovering counterexamples in prior proofs and proposing alternative arguments
items.originalTitle: Classification of Finite Simple Groups Formalized in Lean
items.summary:
A formalization project using the Lean proof assistant has completed the classification of finite simple groups, a major result in group theory. During this process, researchers identified counterexamples to a closure assertion used in an earlier proof approach to the Unbalanced Group Theorem and developed an alternative argument based on Solomon's 1976 theory of maximal 2-components, including a key theorem on the preservation of simple tops.

The work is detailed in a 35-page paper titled "The Unbalanced Group Theorem," which explains the obstruction found in the original proof and presents the new approach for the simple-group case. This formalization effort not only verifies the classification but also contributes new insights to the mathematical theory underlying finite simple groups.

items.title: Researchers extend GEPA optimizer to batch candidate proposals for parallel evaluation, achieving up to fourfold speedups and improved test scores on LiveBench-Math and HoVer tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Batching the Reflective Optimization Loop: Parallel Proposals Make GEPA Faster and Better
items.summary:
Researchers have enhanced the open-source GEPA optimizer by enabling it to propose and evaluate multiple candidates in parallel during each optimization step, rather than sequentially. This approach reduces wall-clock time significantly—most batched runs completed in half the time or less, with the fastest finishing in about a quarter to a third of the original time—and improves held-out test performance on two benchmark tasks, LiveBench-Math and HoVer.

The team developed a runtime model explaining the speedups under a limited worker pool and found that batched optimization uses metric-call and budget resources more efficiently. Their work also outlines the dimensions along which reflective optimization can scale in parallel, providing a framework for allocating fixed optimization budgets across these axes.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.36774v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reflective text optimization makes agentic systems better, but the optimization loop is itself a resource-hungry workload whose sequential structure leaves parallel evaluation capacity idle. We extend the open-source GEPA optimizer to propose and evaluate a batch of candidates on each optimization step instead of one candidate at a time. In our sweep on two tasks, most batched runs finished in half the wall-clock time or less, and the fastest in about a quarter to a third. Batched settings also achieved higher held-out test scores, from 68.9% to 72.1% on LiveBench-Math (with $2\times2$) and from 49.0% to 60.0% on HoVer (with $8\times1$). A simple runtime model explains the measured speedups under a finite worker pool, and batched settings also spend their metric-call and dollar budgets more efficiently. We frame the axes along which a reflective optimization step can scale in parallel, a first look at allocating a fixed optimization budget across them.

items.title: Prospector trains a compact model to traverse scientific knowledge graphs for reasoning, outperforming off-the-shelf models and transferring across domains [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Prospector: learning a compact graph traversal policy for scientific reasoning
items.summary:
Prospector is a compact model trained to perform step-by-step traversal of domain-specific knowledge graphs to support scientific reasoning, addressing limitations of large language models that lack proprietary or specialized data. It progressively builds context by calling a small set of tools and produces evidence chains that can be verified against the graph, achieving performance close to top models on a semiconductor manufacturing knowledge graph and surpassing models that rely on closed-book or preselected graph portions.

Although trained only on semiconductor data, Prospector successfully transfers its traversal policy to knowledge graphs from bio-inspired materials, PFAS, and materials properties fields. It runs efficiently on a single GPU, reducing costs and keeping proprietary data on local hardware. The model's latent state guides its traversal decisions and can be modulated to alter behavior, suggesting a practical approach for combining large language models with knowledge graphs to enable scientific and engineering reasoning over private data.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.37121v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Scientific reasoning in specialized engineering fields depends on knowledge scattered across the literature, often proprietary and absent from frontier LLM training data. In such domains, frontier models tend to give generic answers. Knowledge graphs (KGs) can ground LLM reasoning. Because a graph is too large to provide in full, typical LLM+KG systems preselect a portion, deciding relevance before reasoning begins. Here we train a compact model, Prospector, to reason over a domain knowledge graph by traversing it step by step, seeking evidence in light of what it has already found. Prospector calls a small set of tools one at a time to progressively build its context, and answers with a chain of evidence that can be checked edge by edge against what its tools retrieved from the graph. On a knowledge graph built from the semiconductor-manufacturing literature, Prospector approaches the strongest off-the-shelf models given the same graph and tools, and it far exceeds off-the-shelf models answering closed-book or from a pre-selected portion of the graph. Although trained only on the semiconductor graph, Prospector transfers to unseen knowledge graphs from three other distinct fields: bio-inspired materials, per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) and materials properties. Served on a single GPU, Prospector answers faster and at a fraction of the cost of a hosted service, while keeping proprietary data on the owner's hardware. We find that the policy's latent state is indicative of its next move on both seen and unseen graphs, and modulating the latent state can steer the policy from one behavior mode to another. These results suggest a practical LLM + KG paradigm for scientific and engineering reasoning over private data, in which a compact model trained on a graph from published literature transfers its traversal to unseen graphs that stay with their owners.

items.title: MedJev evaluates zero-shot System One decision model for medical tasks, achieving near GPT-4 accuracy on benchmarks and strong patient-level mortality prediction with local recalibration [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: MedJev: Evaluating Zero-Shot System-One Decision Making in Medicine
items.summary: MedJev is an open System One decision model designed for fast, efficient clinical support by answering structured medical questions without text generation. It was tested across ten medical benchmarks including MedQA, USMLE, and NEJM, achieving accuracies close to GPT-4 and outperforming some supervised models on patient mortality prediction using MIMIC IV datasets. The model runs locally on a laptop and maintains well-calibrated confidence estimates for knowledge tasks but shows miscalibration on patient-level predictions, which the authors address with a lightweight recalibration method using limited labeled data. This work establishes open System One models as promising zero-shot baselines for medical AI, balancing competitive performance with low computational cost, and the authors have released their code and evaluation tools to support further research.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.36006v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: System One decision models such as Jev answer structured questions in a single forward pass without generating text, offering fast and computationally efficient clinical decision support. We evaluate MedJev, an open System One model that runs locally on a laptop, across ten medical benchmarks spanning medical knowledge, diagnosis, and patient level prediction using MIMIC IV and MIMIC IV ED. We compare MedJev against zero shot LLM baselines, published GPT results, and supervised models. MedJev achieves accuracies of 72.5 percent on MedQA, 75.4 percent on USMLE, and 80.1 percent on NEJM, approaching published GPT 4 performance while maintaining well calibrated confidence estimates (ECE 0.028 to 0.063). On patient level tasks, MedJev achieves an AUROC of 0.926 for In Hospital Mortality, exceeding XGBoost (0.902), but underperforms supervised models on operational outcomes such as ED Triage Admission (0.745 vs. 0.809). Patient level predictions also exhibit substantial miscalibration (In Hospital Mortality ECE 0.286). We introduce a lightweight, two parameter recalibration method that adapts predictions to local patient populations using 50 to 200 labeled examples, reducing ECE to 0.007. Our findings establish open System One models as a promising zero shot baseline for medical AI, combining competitive predictive performance with low computational cost and efficient local calibration. We release our code and evaluation harness to support future research.

items.title: Researchers present Fin-SD, a hindsight self-distillation method for multi-step financial reasoning that improves accuracy without external teachers by using student-generated critiques [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: How Much Does the Hint Matter? Scope Conditions for Hindsight Self-Distillation in Financial Reasoning
items.summary: Researchers introduce Fin-SD, a localized hindsight self-distillation technique designed to enhance multi-step financial reasoning in models constrained by data residency. Fin-SD has the student model identify its first incorrect reasoning step, generate a critique, and then distill a hint-conditioned frozen copy of itself to improve accuracy without relying on external teachers. Applied to GPT-OSS-20B on a financial reasoning benchmark, Fin-SD achieves a 3.03 percentage point accuracy gain over the base model and matches traditional self-distillation methods while generating 9.5% fewer tokens. The study finds that the location of supervision matters more than the hint content, and that stronger models do not necessarily provide better hints. Fin-SD maintains performance on general reasoning and compliance audits without regression.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.36082v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Financial institutions operating under data-residency constraints are restricted to open-weight models small enough to locally host, which trail frontier systems on multi-step quantitative reasoning. On-policy distillation narrows such gaps by supervising a student on its own rollouts, but traditional OPD requires a strong external teacher, and on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) conditions on a full reference solution. We ask how much of that signal is necessary. We present Fin-SD, a localized hindsight self-distillation recipe for multi-step reasoning. Given a problem the student fails, the student itself identifies the first incorrect reasoning step and writes a short critique of that step. We truncate the student's trajectory immediately before the error (aiming to obtain a correct prefix), condition a frozen copy of the student on the same prefix plus the hint, and distill that hint-conditioned teacher into the student over a short rollout under reverse KL. No external model contributes a gradient. We apply Fin-SD to GPT-OSS-20B on a custom multi-step financial reasoning benchmark that requires deriving formula inputs from realistic scenarios via accounting conventions. We find: (i) replacing the critique with a generic-feedback control matches Fin-SD's entire 3.03 pp accuracy gain over the base model on the FinanceReasoning Hard subset, suggesting the gain comes from where supervision is applied, not hint content; (ii) the model writing the hint does not need to be stronger than the model receiving it: hints from same-family GPT-OSS-120B, at roughly 6x the parameters, yield no materially greater benefits than self-written hints; and (iii) Fin-SD matches on-policy self-distillation from full reference solutions on accuracy while generating 9.5% fewer tokens. With Fin-SD, general reasoning on MMLU-Pro and a fourteen-metric compliance audit on FinTrust show no material regression.

items.title: Researchers show base pre-trained models can detect hidden intentions in outputs that prompted classifiers miss using persona-header likelihood evaluation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Base Models Can Detect Hidden Intentions that Prompted Classifiers Miss
items.summary: Researchers propose the Persona Selection Model (PSM) and introduce persona-header likelihood evaluation (PHLE) to decode subliminal signals embedded in model outputs, such as number sequences reflecting covert prompts like "You love owls" versus "You love eagles." PHLE distinguishes these signals even when prompted classifiers, including the generating model, perform near chance. The method also detects hidden harmful intents in filtered model responses and shows signal persistence across different model families, suggesting practical applications for auditing hidden model objectives.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.36202v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Persona Selection Model (PSM) posits that post-training selects a persona the model learned during pre-training. Work on subliminal learning has shown that models can impart covert signals (like "love of owls") into semantically unrelated outputs like strings of numbers, and that students trained on these outputs inherit those traits. In this work I show that by evaluating the likelihood of such outputs under the base pre-trained model with an appropriate header, a method I call persona-header likelihood evaluation (PHLE), one can decode these subliminal signals and classify between them. For example, PHLE distinguishes number sequences generated by a post-trained model prompted with "You love owls" from those prompted with "You love eagles", and distinguishes answers from a model with a secret desire to harm the user, filtered to remove any noticeable misalignment, from those of a model with no system prompt. In both cases prompted classifiers, including the generating model itself, remain near chance. The signal partially persists across model families, with the Qwen base model reading signals generated by Olmo and vice versa. This is evidence for a non-trivial prediction of the PSM, and the method may be practically useful for auditing the hidden objectives of models.

items.title: RoboAuto introduces a multi-level physical understanding framework for autonomous robot program search, achieving up to 89.1% success on LIBERO-PRO tasks and outperforming prior methods on long-horizon manipulation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: RoboAuto: Autonomous Robot Program Search through Multi-Level Physical Understanding
items.summary: RoboAuto is a new framework for autonomous robot program search that integrates physical understanding at the object, scene, and interaction levels. It uses a hierarchical knowledge base combining executable skills with object-centric knowledge, scene grounding to connect knowledge to the environment, and multi-stage planning with self-designed experiments to test physical effects and resolve uncertainties. This approach enables superior performance on five benchmark families, including an 89.1% success rate on short-horizon LIBERO-PRO tasks and more than double the success rate of ASPIRE on long-horizon LIBERO-PRO Long and LIBERO-Plus tasks. RoboAuto also outperforms ASPIRE and π₀.₅ on challenging real-robot tasks requiring precise manipulation. The knowledge base transfers across simulators and robot embodiments, and program search performance improves with knowledge base size.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.36533v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recently, LLM-based autonomous agents have shown strong capabilities in iteratively generating, evaluating, and refining executable solutions. In robotic manipulation, Code-as-Policy lets these agents search over modular and editable robot programs. However, effective program search requires physical understanding: agents must understand how objects can be manipulated, how scene geometry constrains actions, and why interactions succeed or fail. Existing methods rely mainly on execution feedback for program refinement, often leaving these physical questions unresolved. We introduce RoboAuto, a framework for robot program search that explicitly organizes physical understanding at the object, scene, and interaction levels through three components. First, a hierarchical knowledge base combines executable skills with object-centric knowledge of affordances, spatial relations, and action effects, learned from embodied data and online task solving. Second, scene grounding connects this knowledge to the current environment by identifying relevant objects and resolving action-critical quantities. Third, multi-stage planning with self-designed experiments checks whether each stage produces its expected physical effects and actively tests competing hypotheses to resolve physical uncertainties. RoboAuto achieves superior performance across five benchmark families, attaining an 89.1% success rate on short-horizon LIBERO-PRO tasks and more than twice the mean success rate of ASPIRE on LIBERO-PRO Long and LIBERO-Plus. It also outperforms ASPIRE and $\pi_{0.5}$ on three challenging long-horizon real-robot tasks requiring precise manipulation. We further show that the knowledge base transfers across simulators and embodiments, and that program search performance scales with its size. Project page: https://roboauto-ai.github.io/

items.title: Researchers propose Balanced State Subspaces and HARP for Mamba-2 state compression, halving state dimension with minimal perplexity increase on WikiText-2 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Balanced State Subspaces for Mamba-2 State Compression
items.summary:
Researchers introduce a post-training transform called Balanced State Subspaces for Mamba-2, a model that compresses context into a fixed-size recurrent state dominating decoding memory and bandwidth. They find that existing compression methods miss key directions in the state space and propose targeting the write-read subspace instead. To address varying useful ranks across layers, they also introduce HARP, which allocates ranks per layer based on the Hankel spectrum and protects retrieval-sensitive layers, improving perplexity and retrieval performance compared to uniform budgets.

The proposed method applies balanced truncation using full controllability and observability Gramians and leverages Mamba-2's scalar-identity transition for exact rotation. Calibration requires only a single forward pass, making it significantly faster and more memory-efficient than previous protocols like GHOST. Experiments show that with HARP, the state dimension can be halved with an average perplexity increase of 0.3 points (1.8%) on WikiText-2 across model sizes from 130 million to 2.7 billion parameters, outperforming GHOST's 1.6 point (9.3%) increase, with the performance gap widening at 25% retention.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.36617v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mamba-2 compresses all context into a fixed-size recurrent state that dominates decoding memory and bandwidth. Existing compressors quantize state values or prune state coordinates, scoring each channel independently in the native basis. We examine trained Mamba-2 states and find that energy is almost rank-one, but the output does not read the energetic directions: energy concentrates in a bias-like direction accumulated by the recurrence, while the content the output reads lives in a low-dimensional subspace that is not aligned with the state's coordinates. Even output-aware scores are computed coordinate by coordinate, so they miss the directions that determine the input--output map. Compression should therefore target the write--read subspace rather than individual coordinates. We propose \method{}, a post-training transform that instantiates balanced truncation with full controllability and observability Gramians and applies the rotation exactly via Mamba-2's scalar-identity transition. Because the useful rank varies widely across layers, we further introduce HARP, which allocates ranks per layer from the Hankel spectrum and protects retrieval-sensitive layers, improving both perplexity and retrieval over uniform budgets. Calibration takes a single forward pass, an order of magnitude faster than GHOST's released protocol, with lower peak memory. With HARP, \method{} halves the state dimension at an average WikiText-2 perplexity increase of $0.3$ points ($1.8\%$) across 130M--2.7B, versus $1.6$ ($9.3\%$) for GHOST, and the gap widens at 25\% retention.

items.title: Researchers train small GPT-2 models on child speech transcripts and synthetic dialogues to study language learning from limited, naturalistic data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Specialization, Diversity, and Scaling in Child-Scale Language Models
items.summary: Researchers trained small GPT-2 language models on transcripts of child speech from dense home recordings and synthetic child-directed dialogues, varying the amount, source, and diversity of training data to investigate language learning from small datasets. Models trained on one child's language environment predicted that environment better than others, with specialization largely lexical and distributional, and training on multiple children's data improved prediction of pooled language but not grammatical benchmarks. The study found that naturalistic and synthetic inputs produce different grammatical and lexical-semantic patterns, highlighting that small-data language learning depends on both the quantity and the match of input environments to the prediction task.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.36679v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern language models are trained on far more language than children experience, but we know much less about learning from small, naturalistic datasets. We train small GPT-2 models on transcripts of speech with children from dense home recordings (BabyView) and on synthetic child-directed dialogue (TinyDialogues), varying the amount, source, and diversity of training data. Models trained on one child's language environment predict that environment substantially better than other children's environments. Much of this specialization is lexical and distributional: a simple 5-gram model reproduces the cross-child pattern (r=.91). Training on data from multiple children clearly improves prediction of pooled held-out language relative to training on a single child's input without a similarly clear improvement on grammatical benchmarks. Across data sizes, naturalistic and synthetic training inputs also produce different grammatical and lexical-semantic patterns, with important differences between grammatical phenomena. Together, these results show that small-data language learning depends not only on how much language a model sees, but on which environments it comes from and how well that input matches what the model is asked to predict.

items.title: Select-TTT introduces query-conditioned selective fast weight updates for in-place test-time training, improving long-context question answering on multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Select-TTT: Query-Conditioned Selective Fast Weight Updates for In-Place Test-Time Training
items.summary: Select-TTT is a new method that enhances in-place test-time training (TTT) for language models by selectively scaling fast weight updates based on the relevance of context chunks to the user query. Unlike previous uniform update approaches, Select-TTT uses a relevance signal derived from the model's frozen output head without additional parameters or supervision. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.36794v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Test-time training (TTT) enables a deployed language model to internalize incoming context on-the-fly into a small set of fast-weight parameters, rather than merely treating it as transient context for attention. In-Place TTT recently made this idea practical for large language models by repurposing the down-projection of standard MLP blocks as fast weights. However, we find that its benefit largely disappears on realistic web long-context question answering. We attribute this to In-Place TTT's uniform write schedule: every chunk is written with equal strength, so irrelevant content dilutes query-relevant information in fast-weight memory. Building on this insight, we propose Select-TTT, a model-agnostic, query-conditioned rule for In-Place TTT that scales each chunk's write strength by its relevance to the user query. This relevance signal requires no supervision and no new parameters: it is read directly from the model's frozen output head, as the probability mass that a chunk's hidden states assign to the query tokens. A temperature-scaled softmax turns these scores into learning-rate multipliers, leaving the chunk-wise, context-parallel computation of In-Place TTT intact. Select-TTT consistently improves long-context question answering on two benchmarks and two backbones. These findings highlight the value of query-conditioned fast weight writes for practical test-time training on long-context question answering, which is also potentially promising for long-horizon agent tasks involving multiple user queries over evolving contexts.

items.title: Researchers introduce V-LUMEN, a visual lookup memory system that discretizes visual features to expand capacity in vision-language models without increasing compute [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: V-LUMEN: Visual Lookup Memory for Embedding Scaling in Vision-Language Models
items.summary: V-LUMEN is a new approach that applies embedding-level scaling to vision-language models by discretizing continuous visual features using a frozen codebook and spatially aware hashing. It integrates retrieved embeddings into model backbones through a gated residual pathway, improving performance on reasoning-intensive benchmarks and enabling zero-shot transfer to unseen image datasets. The method maintains accuracy while shifting capacity from adapters to external visual memory, which grows storage requirements rather than per-token computation, and the code has been made publicly available.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.37019v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Embedding-level scaling expands the capacity of language models through lookup-based memory rather than by increasing model depth, width, or dense computation. Extending this idea to vision-language models (VLMs) is challenging because visual features are continuous, spatially structured, and query-dependent, unlike discrete text tokens that naturally support n-gram lookup. We introduce V-LUMEN, a visual lookup memory for VLMs. V-LUMEN discretizes visual features with a frozen codebook, builds spatially aware memory keys through spatial aggregation-based hashing, and modulates them with text-conditioned relevance signals; all addressing is non-parametric, and the retrieved embeddings are fused into the backbone through a gated residual pathway. On five reasoning-intensive benchmarks, V-LUMEN substantially improves a frozen Qwen3-VL-2B backbone and transfers zero-shot to three benchmarks whose images are disjoint from the training data. At a matched parameter budget, moving part of a LoRA or MoE adapter's capacity into V-LUMEN preserves accuracy on two backbones, indicating that external visual memory is an independent capacity axis rather than a stronger adaptation method. Because lookup cost is constant in table size and incurred only once at prefill, this capacity grows in storage rather than in per-token compute. Code is available at https://github.com/miso-choi/V-Lumen.

items.originalTitle: Zooming without Zooming v2: From Seeing Details to Connecting Evidence for Generalizable Multimodal Perception
items.summary: Researchers introduce EvidenceConnect, a data synthesis framework that generates questions requiring comparison and aggregation of visual evidence from zoomed regions within single images to enhance multimodal perception. They train vision-language models using this data with reinforcement learning, resulting in Zooming without Zooming v2 (ZwZ2), which improves fine-grained spatial perception and multimodal reasoning tasks without being tailored to specific benchmarks. The approach demonstrates that strengthening the capability to connect visual evidence leads to more generalizable multimodal intelligence.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.37037v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multimodal perception forms the foundation of multimodal intelligence. In particular, spatial perception and multimodal long-context understanding are two pivotal tasks that underpin embodied AI and multimodal agents. However, synthesizing targeted, high-quality training data for these tasks remains difficult and costly. Our key insight is that these tasks share an underlying capability, which we call connecting evidence: identifying relevant visual facts, binding them to the correct entities, recovering their relations, and composing them into an answer. Crucially, targeted training data are far easier to synthesize for this capability than for these tasks themselves. To strengthen this capability, we propose EvidenceConnect, an easy-to-implement data synthesis framework that uses zoomed views of related regions within a single image to generate questions requiring comparison, aggregation, or chaining of visual evidence. To ensure quality, a reference answer is retained only when independent VLMs agree on it, and region-ablation tests discard questions whose answer survives the removal of selected regions. We then train base VLMs on the resulting data with RLVR, obtaining Zooming without Zooming v2 (ZwZ2). Although the synthesized data are not tailored to any downstream benchmark, ZwZ2 improves fine-grained and spatial perception, with further gains on embodied spatial reasoning, multimodal long-context understanding, multimodal agent tasks, and general visual reasoning. These results establish EvidenceConnect as an effective framework for supervising evidence connection and suggest that strengthening this shared capability leads to more generalizable multimodal perception.

items.title: Researchers find single-pair model biases limit Direct Preference Optimization performance compared to multi-model data, highlighting generator diversity as key [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Exploring the Limits of the Delta Learning Hypothesis: Single-Pair Generator Biases in Direct Preference Optimization
items.summary:
Researchers investigated the delta-learning hypothesis in Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), which suggests supervision can come from a single pair of models by preferring the larger model's response. They found that fixed model pairs introduce systematic biases that predict preference labels independent of response quality, causing DPO trained on single-pair data to underperform compared to multi-model preference data despite higher-quality responses from larger models.

The study combined theoretical and empirical analysis across model families and scales, tracing performance gaps to training dynamics consistent with reward hacking on these biases. Increasing the number of generators, even without an external judge, partially mitigated these effects, underscoring the importance of generator diversity in constructing preference data for DPO.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.37058v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) typically relies on preference pairs generated from diverse model pools and ranked by an external LLM judge. The recently proposed delta-learning hypothesis suggests that comparable supervision can instead be obtained from a single pair of models by treating the larger model's response as preferred. We investigate the limits of this approach across model families and scales. We show, both theoretically and empirically, that fixed model pairs introduce systematic, generator-dependent biases that are predictive of the preference label independent of response quality. Consequently, DPO trained on single-pair data consistently underperforms multi-model preference data, despite the larger generator producing higher-quality responses, and we trace this gap to training dynamics consistent with reward hacking on these biases. We further show that simply increasing the number of generators, even without an external judge, is enough to partially mitigate this effect. Our results highlight generator diversity as a critical factor in preference-data construction.

items.title: Researchers introduce EnergyCal to reduce loss spikes in Muon-family optimizers for sparse MoE training, achieving over 95% spike reduction on a 4B-parameter model [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: EnergyCal: Taming Loss Spikes in Muon-Family Optimizers for Sparse MoE Training
items.summary: Researchers present EnergyCal, a lightweight method that attenuates routed-expert updates based on normalized squared Frobenius norms to stabilize sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) language-model training with Muon-family optimizers. Evaluated on a 4-billion-parameter MoE model, EnergyCal reduced mean thresholded loss-spike burden by 99.51% and improved final perplexity by 4.06% compared to a lower-learning-rate MuonH baseline, with modest throughput cost. The method does not alter the spectral transform or add persistent optimizer state. Results also show over 95% spike reduction with plain Muon optimizer at matched learning rates, supporting stabilization both with and without Hyperball in the tested setting.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.37062v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) language-model training can exhibit large loss spikes with Muon-family optimizers. We introduce EnergyCal, a lightweight rule that attenuates routed-expert updates according to the normalized squared Frobenius norm of their finite-step Newton-Schulz directions. EnergyCal leaves the spectral transform unchanged and adds no persistent optimizer state. We evaluate it on a 4B-parameter MoE model. Against a development-selected, lower-learning-rate MuonH recipe, EnergyCal-MuonH reduces mean thresholded loss-spike burden by 99.51% and final geometric-mean perplexity by 4.06%, with a modest throughput cost. With plain Muon at matched nominal learning rate and weight decay, the reduction in mean spike burden averages 95.98% across the two tested exponents, accompanied by small endpoint improvements. These findings support stabilization both with and without Hyperball in the evaluated setting.

items.title: Researchers propose EvalAlloc framework to optimize evaluation budget allocation in LLM-driven agent scaffold evolution, achieving higher performance with half the evaluations [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Where Should the Evaluation Budget Go in LLM-Driven Agent Scaffold Evolution?
items.summary:
Researchers investigate how to allocate evaluation budgets in large language model (LLM)-driven agent scaffold evolution, which improves agent workflows through iterative candidate generation and evaluation but incurs high execution costs when evaluating every candidate fully. They find that sparse feedback can sustain productive evolution, while targeted evaluation enhances final selection, and propose EvalAlloc, a framework combining sparse search-time feedback with targeted final confirmation to optimize evaluation efficiency.

EvalAlloc uses a short fully evaluated warm-up to establish a shared informative core and calibrate a response model, then applies paired successive halving after search to reuse observations and execute only missing evaluations. Tested across four benchmarks and two evolution frameworks, EvalAlloc achieves higher mean performance than full evaluation in most settings while using approximately half as many evaluation cells, indicating a more efficient approach to managing evaluation costs in LLM-driven agent development.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.37276v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-driven agent scaffold evolution improves agent workflows through iterative candidate generation and evaluation. Evaluation both guides subsequent search and determines the final scaffold, but evaluating every candidate on the full task set incurs substantial execution costs. We investigate how evaluation budgets can be allocated across these two roles. Our experiments show that sparse feedback can sustain productive evolution, while additional targeted evaluation improves final selection. Replay analyses further show that shared informative items and a common scoring reference support comparisons among closely matched candidates. Motivated by these findings, we propose \method, an evaluation allocation framework that combines sparse search-time feedback with targeted final confirmation. A short fully evaluated warm-up establishes a shared informative core and calibrates a response model whose item parameters remain fixed during search. After search, \method refits the model and applies paired successive halving, reusing accumulated observations and executing only missing evaluations. Across four benchmarks and two evolution frameworks, \method achieves higher mean performance than full evaluation in most settings while using approximately half as many evaluation cells.

items.title: Researchers develop SimpleLoRIF to trace safety degradation in fine-tuned LLMs by identifying training examples aligned with unsafe behavior, enabling safer dataset filtering [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Follow the Gradient: Tracing Safety Degradation Back to Training Data
items.summary:
Researchers have developed SimpleLoRIF, a scalable gradient embedding method that identifies fine-tuning examples in large language models (LLMs) whose gradients align with unsafe behavior, addressing the challenge of safety degradation from seemingly benign training data. By simplifying a low-rank attribution method and limiting backpropagation to the final transformer blocks, SimpleLoRIF can process datasets with up to a million examples, making gradient attribution practical for full post-training datasets.

The team validated SimpleLoRIF on emergent misalignment scenarios, showing it can link insecure-code training data to harmful behaviors after fine-tuning with high accuracy. Using this method, they created SafeTulu, a filtered version of Tulu 3 that removes the 20% of examples most aligned with unsafe responses, reducing attack success rates by up to 22% across multiple models while maintaining or improving capabilities. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.37481v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fine-tuning Large Language Models (LLMs) on instruction data can quietly erode their safety, even when no training example looks harmful. Because this safety-degrading data looks benign, standard content filters struggle to catch it. We tackle this problem by developing SimpleLoRIF, a scalable gradient embedding method that identifies fine-tuning examples whose gradients align with unsafe behavior. By simplifying a low-rank attribution method and restricting backpropagation to the final four transformer blocks, SimpleLoRIF can embed datasets on the order of a million examples, boosting gradient attribution from a small-scale analysis tool into a practical filter for full post-training datasets. We first validate it on emergent misalignment, where we find that gradients can connect insecure-code training data to the broadly harmful behaviors that appear after fine-tuning, with AUC as high as 0.865 in the gradient space of misaligned models. We then use SimpleLoRIF to build SafeTulu, a version of Tulu 3 with the 20% of examples most gradient-aligned with unsafe responses removed. Training on SafeTulu reduces GCG attack success rate by up to 22% across Qwen, Llama, and Olmo, outperforming both LLM-as-a-judge and prior gradient-based filtering, while largely preserving or even improving capability. Finally, we analyzed the removed data and identify possibly under-studied sources of safety degradation, such as tool-execution failures and narrative arithmetic. We release SafeTulu along with a Hugging Face Space that lets researchers build their own customized versions of SafeTulu to fine-tune on, such as by changing the removal fraction or filtering only certain subsets.

items.title: Validating FKG.in: Soundness Assessment in LLM-Augmented Indian Food Knowledge [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Validating FKG.in: Soundness Assessment in LLM-Augmented Indian Food Knowledge
items.summary: arXiv:2608.29249v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The online culinary ecosystem is increasingly populated by recipe content generated, modified, or summarized by LLMs. Although often convincing, such outputs may contain hallucinated ingredients, misrepresented quantities, or culturally implausible combinations, limiting their suitability for downstream applications and knowledge graph construction. In this paper, we present a semi-automated soundness assessment workflow for validating structured recipe data extracted from informal culinary sources and augmented by LLMs. Developed as part of FKG(.in), a knowledge graph of Indian food, the pipeline identifies and addresses common failure modes, including structural inconsistencies, semantic and logical incoherence, and deviations from the source text, through a multi-stage process combining formal grammars, vocabulary-based checks, statistical heuristics, Set Transformer-based coherence modeling, and retrieval-based verification. Although evaluated on Indian recipes, the proposed methods are applicable to broader multilingual and multicultural culinary domains. We provide a practical, auditable, and application-agnostic approach to improving the reliability of machine-readable food knowledge infrastructures in the era of LLM-generated content.

items.title: Fairness Definitions in Language Models Explained [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Fairness Definitions in Language Models Explained
items.summary: arXiv:2407.18454v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Language Models (LMs) have demonstrated exceptional performance across various Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks. Despite these advancements, LMs can inherit and amplify societal biases related to sensitive attributes such as gender and race, limiting their adoption in real-world applications. Therefore, fairness has been extensively explored in LMs, leading to the proposal of various fairness notions. However, the lack of clear agreement on which fairness definition to apply in specific contexts and the complexity of understanding the distinctions between these definitions can create confusion and impede further progress. To this end, this paper proposes a systematic survey that clarifies the definitions of fairness as they apply to LMs. Specifically, we begin with a brief introduction to LMs and fairness in LMs, followed by a comprehensive, up-to-date overview of existing fairness notions in LMs and the introduction of a novel taxonomy that categorizes these concepts based on their transformer architecture: encoder-only, decoder-only, and encoder-decoder LMs. We further illustrate each definition through experiments, showcasing their practical implications and outcomes. Finally, we discuss current research challenges and open questions, aiming to foster innovative ideas and advance the field. The repository is publicly available online at https://github.com/vanbanTruong/Fairness-in-Large-Language-Models/tree/main/definitions.

items.title: An Embarrassingly Simple Data Selection Strategy for Million-Scale Multi-Modal Instruction-Tuning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: An Embarrassingly Simple Data Selection Strategy for Million-Scale Multi-Modal Instruction-Tuning
items.summary: arXiv:2503.13383v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recent research demonstrates that pretrained large language models (LLMs) require minimal but carefully curated data for instruction-tuning. Building on LLMs, multi-modal models further contend with far larger data volumes, heterogeneous sources, and cross-modal alignment, amplifying both the necessity and the complexity of data selection. However, existing methods rely on deeply extracted embeddings, gradients or narrow quality scores that are time-consuming to compute and limited in expressiveness, frequently failing to surpass a simple random-sampling baseline. To overcome these limitations, we step back from complex embedding spaces and target the fundamental objective of instruction tuning: how and what knowledge should be elicited from the pretrained model and exposed to users. We leverage interaction \underline{S}tyles as a proxy for structural diversity, and decompose data quality into capability-specific \underline{S}cores, yielding an explicit yet \underline{R}ich (SSR) profile for each sample. We further cast the selection as submodular coverage maximization over the capability--style grid, providing an approximation guarantee. SSR consistently delivers superior performance across two distinct architecture stacks, LLaVA-1.5 (Vicuna + CLIP) and LLaVA-OneVision (Qwen2 + SigLIP), two large-scale data pools, six data budget settings, and 14 multi-modal benchmarks. To our knowledge, SSR is the first data selection method validated at million-scale, achieving 99.1% of full-data performance using only 30% of a 2.6M pool. Furthermore, the SSR profile models and selected subsets transfer training-free across data pools and model architectures with capability extensibility.

items.title: SELF: A Robust Singular Value and Eigenvalue Approach for LLM Fingerprinting [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: SELF: A Robust Singular Value and Eigenvalue Approach for LLM Fingerprinting
items.summary: arXiv:2512.03620v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Safeguarding the Intellectual Property (IP) of Large Language Models (LLMs) against model theft represents a critical challenge in contemporary AI research. Although fingerprinting is essential for establishing forensic evidence for model derivation, existing methods are susceptible to false claim attacks, weight manipulations, or high false positive rates, undermining their utility. To overcome these limitations, we propose SELF, \rev{a novel intrinsic weight-based fingerprinting scheme tailored for robust IP forensics via adversarial model lineage verification}. SELF eliminates dependency on input and inherently resists false claims, achieving robust \rev{provenance detection} through unique, scalable and transformation-invariant fingerprint extraction via singular value and eigenvalue decomposition of LLM attention weights. Experimental results demonstrate that SELF maintains high IP infringement detection accuracy while significantly outperforming state-of-the-art baselines in reducing false positives and showing strong robustness against various downstream modifications, including quantization, pruning, and fine-tuning attacks. Our code is available at https://github.com/HanxiuZhang/SELF_v4.

items.title: Counting Clues: A Lightweight Probabilistic Baseline Can Match an LLM [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Counting Clues: A Lightweight Probabilistic Baseline Can Match an LLM
items.summary: arXiv:2512.12868v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel on multiple-choice clinical diagnosis benchmarks, yet it is unclear how much of this performance reflects underlying probabilistic reasoning. We study this through questions from MedQA that ask for the most likely diagnosis. We introduce Frequency-Based Probabilistic Ranker (FBPR), a lightweight method that scores options with a smoothed Naive Bayes over concept-diagnosis co-occurrence statistics from a large corpus. When co-occurrence statistics are sourced from Dolma, the pretraining corpus for OLMo, and RedPajama, an open reproduction of the LLaMA pretraining-data recipe, FBPR achieves comparable performance to the corresponding LLMs. Furthermore, direct LLM inference and FBPR exhibit complementary strengths, correctly answering largely different subsets of questions with overlap barely above chance. Combining them with a simple hybrid method yields a notable gain over either method alone. These findings show that explicit probabilistic baselines can account for a substantial portion of the benchmark performance on diagnosis questions, while serving as historically grounded reference points and complementary signals for hybridization.

We introduce Frequency-Based Probabilistic Ranker (FBPR), a lightweight method that scores options with a smoothed Naive Bayes over concept-diagnosis co-occurrence statistics from a large corpus. When co-occurrence statistics are sourced from Dolma, the pretraining corpus for OLMo, and RedPajama, an open reproduction of the LLaMA pretraining-data recipe, FBPR achieves comparable performance to the corresponding LLMs. Furthermore, direct LLM inference and FBPR exhibit complementary strengths, correctly answering largely different subsets of questions with overlap barely above chance. Combining them with a simple hybrid method yields a notable gain over either method alone. These findings show that explicit probabilistic baselines can account for a substantial portion of the benchmark performance on diagnosis questions, while serving as historically grounded reference points and complementary signals for hybridization.

items.title: The Geometry of Learning: Read-Write Asymmetry Across Training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Geometry of Learning: Read-Write Asymmetry Across Training
items.summary: arXiv:2605.16600v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Pretraining and alignment update the same transformer weights, and we ask in which directions each stage changes them. The residual stream gives every matrix a shared coordinate system, in which a weight change can be compared with the principal subspace of the activations the matrix reads and with the prediction subspace of the unembedding. In this frame, alignment updates to the query and key matrices are enriched in the principal input subspace, while its updates to the output matrices are close to random relative to the prediction subspace, and the same signature appears in late pretraining and under every objective we apply to one checkpoint, so it is a property of the training stage rather than of the objective. The gradient of a linear map is a sum of outer products $\delta_t a_t^\top$, and the residual stream enters this product through the activation $a_t$ for matrices that read from it and through the upstream gradient $\delta_t$ for matrices that write into it. Read gradients therefore inherit the spectrum of the activations, which is the same under every objective, while write gradients inherit the geometry of the upstream gradients, which point into the prediction subspace only early in pretraining, when the output matrices acquire their prediction geometry. The raw read gradient follows the activation spectrum, the optimiser attenuates the concentration it inherits, and cancellation between tokens sets the scale of the update but not its direction. A write direction derived from the unembedding still changes predictions after alignment, and adaptation restricted to any single group of matrices remains effective, so the signature describes where training places its updates, not which matrices can carry them.

items.title: Does The Way You Plan Matter? An Empirical Study of Planning Representations for LLM Web Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Does The Way You Plan Matter? An Empirical Study of Planning Representations for LLM Web Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2605.29927v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Despite recent advances, LLM-based web agents still struggle with limited exploration, omission of critical steps, and sensitivity to task constraints. Prior work suggests that many of these failures stem from weaknesses in planning, yet the impact of alternative natural language plan representations remains unexplored. To address this, we introduce PlanAhead, a static planner-executor framework that evaluates the impact of plan representation on agent performance. We first automatically categorize WebArena tasks into 3 difficulty levels, enabling consistent difficulty grading without human annotation. Then we systematically evaluate 4 different plan representations on the tasks categorized as hard: sequential subgoals, narrative, pseudocode, and checklist; across different families of multimodal LLM-powered agents(OpenAI, Alibaba, and Google). To account for stochastic variability, we introduce a novel decomposition of agent Success Rate (SR) into 2 interpretable evaluation metrics: Achievement Rate (AR) and Solved-Task Consistency (STC). Our results show that both, the plan formulation and the underlying LLM generating the plan, significantly influence web-agent robustness and task success.

items.title: TextCloak: Safeguarding Data from Unauthorized LLM Fine-Tuning via RL-Driven Unlearnable Examples [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: TextCloak: Safeguarding Data from Unauthorized LLM Fine-Tuning via RL-Driven Unlearnable Examples
items.summary: arXiv:2607.28862v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The development of Large Language Models (LLMs) has led to significant advances across a wide range of language tasks, while simultaneously raising growing concerns about unauthorized online data exploitation and privacy leakage. Unlearnable examples (UEs) emerge as a promising defense by injecting crafted perturbations into data such that models trained on them exhibit degraded utility. However, existing methods for text protection are primarily designed for classification tasks and discriminative language models, which limits their broad applicability (e.g., instruction following or reasoning) in LLMs. In this work, we propose **TextCloak**, an RL-driven data synthesis framework that safeguards textual data against unauthorized LLM fine-tuning. TextCloak employs a *UE generative policy* that transforms clean text into unlearnable examples while preserving semantic fidelity and linguistic naturalness. To optimize the policy, we introduce **GRPO-UE**, which simulates the attacker's LLM fine-tuning and rewards downstream degradation via group-relative policy optimization. This overall formulates a bi-level optimization loop, allowing the generator to discover effective protective patterns. Comprehensive experiments on six publicly available datasets and nine state-of-the-art LLMs demonstrate that TextCloak consistently impairs unauthorized LLM fine-tuning while maintaining text utility for legitimate use. Further analyses confirm its transferability and robustness across model architectures, training configurations, and adaptive attacks, highlighting its broad applicability as a practical defense for online content.

items.title: The Score Is Not the Structure: Brain Alignment and Cross-Lingual Transfer [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Score Is Not the Structure: Brain Alignment and Cross-Lingual Transfer
items.summary: arXiv:2610.03827v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Similarity scores are often offered as evidence that a model shares structure with the brain or across languages. We ask what such a score reads when that structure is removed, or when the instrument measuring it does not work, in two settings. Across seventeen languages, a grammaticality probe transfers worse between more distant languages (r = -0.66). But the probe's own accuracy falls along the same axis and is at chance in four languages, four of the five most distant. Dropping them halves the explained variance, and because it also narrows the range of distances, the design cannot say how much of the gradient is the instrument. Counting the 272 language pairs as independent gives p = 0.0006 for a steering effect that is null when the seventeen languages are the unit (p = 0.155). In brain alignment, a training objective raises a language model's similarity to fMRI responses from 0.10 to 0.34 (reliability ceiling 0.54), yet targets with the brain correspondence destroyed still reach 0.31. A shuffled target scores about k/n against the real one, for rank k and n sentences, a baseline that can be computed before any model is trained. Both interventions work, yet we detect no distance-graded steering effect and no syntactic benefit from alignment. Before reading a correspondence score, measure how much of it survives without the correspondence.

items.title: Agaram 2.5B: The First Tamil-First Language Model Trained from Scratch with Tool Calling. A Playbook for Under-Represented Languages [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Agaram 2.5B: The First Tamil-First Language Model Trained from Scratch with Tool Calling. A Playbook for Under-Represented Languages
items.summary: arXiv:2610.18420v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present Agaram 2.5B, a Tamil-first language model trained from scratch that converses in Tamil script, romanized Tanglish and English, and calls tools. Our first model, Agaram 1.5B, guided the new base, tokenizer and fine-tuning recipe: we pretrained a new 2.53B-parameter base on 50 billion tokens, 58% of them Tamil, with a tokenizer that needs 1.55 tokens per Tamil word where Qwen2.5's needs 9.44. A four-day public preview of our first 2.5B chat model showed where it fell short with real users, and we rebuilt supervised fine-tuning around what we saw, on 222,662 records. The released model scores above Sarvam-1 in all six translation directions we measured (FLORES chrF 56.9 into Tamil and 55.4 into English), chooses the expected tool on all 25 prompts of a tool set that was used during checkpoint selection and whose schemas appear in training, with exact arguments on 16, and was preferred over the preview model by an LLM judge on 100 sealed human-written prompts (net preference +30 points, 95% interval +14.5 to +45.0). On FLORES it also scores above Google's Gemma 4 E4B-it and our fine-tuned variant of it in both directions, with 2.53B parameters against E4B's 4.5B effective parameters. Factual knowledge and reliable refusal of harmful requests remain open problems, which we set out as future work. The base and chat weights and GGUF files are released under Apache-2.0, and this report gives a full account of the data, training and evaluation as a playbook for building language models for under-represented languages.

items.title: Quantitative Generalization Bounds for Multi-Layer Transformers: A Few Long Strings can Beat Many Short Ones [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Quantitative Generalization Bounds for Multi-Layer Transformers: A Few Long Strings can Beat Many Short Ones
items.summary: arXiv:2610.35715v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Transformer-based language models exhibit an astonishing capacity to generalize to longer and more difficult problem instances than those seen in training. However, theoretical understanding of this phenomenon still lags behind. Unlike most machine learning models, the generalisation abilities of transformers inherently require considering two axes. On one hand, one must examine in-distribution statistical generalisation, which concerns the ability of a model to broaden a function from training samples to novel samples of the same distribution. On the other hand, given the sequential nature of language data, one must also consider length generalisation, which reflects whether a model trained on inputs of a given length can extrapolate to longer ones. These two notions have mostly been studied separately, leaving open how they interact. In this work, we give a joint treatment of both axes for fixed-precision transformers. We give generalisation guarantees in terms of the parameter sizes of the involved models, as well as the quantization space and the alphabet size that supply the sequences. Finally, we illustrate how the requirements in the sample count and training length trade off. In particular, we find that increasing training length can be exponentially more efficient than increasing the sample size. Experiments support predictions of the theory.

items.title: Don't Pick a Winner: Knowledge Conflicts Need a Prior, Not a Rule [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Don't Pick a Winner: Knowledge Conflicts Need a Prior, Not a Rule
items.summary: arXiv:2610.36169v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A retrieval-augmented language model answers from two sources, the retrieved context and its own knowledge, and the two disagree whenever the context is incomplete or wrong. Existing methods settle the disagreement with a rule fixed at design time: follow the context, amplify it in proportion to how far it moves the model, or trust the model's memory. Each rule is confidently wrong in some deployment. In a decision-theoretic model of two sources, the score of any fixed rule is linear in the share of reliable contexts while the best attainable score is convex, so every fixed rule is beaten wherever it is not exactly optimal; and a symmetric divergence between the two sources, the signal adaptive decoding uses, carries no information about which one is right. Resolving a conflict therefore needs two inputs that no existing method keeps: evidence about each source separately, and a prior on how often the context is right. We test these claims on GRACE, a benchmark that intervenes on the knowledge-graph context of a fixed question, so that what the model knows, what the context says and what is true are measured separately. There, every baseline from four families is strong on right contexts or on wrong ones, never on both. We then build the two inputs: the model states its knowledge as notes, a small policy voices each note with a calibrated confidence, a reader answers in two voices, and a selector commits or abstains under a prior $\pi$ applied as an exact prior shift. With $\pi$ set to the true share of right contexts, the system is above the best baseline at every mixture of GRACE contexts, by up to 26 points. Its overall score is 45.3 and 35.0 (Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, Llama-3.1-8B), against 29.4 and 27.5 for the best baseline. On preregistered ClashEval it beats same-backbone CK-PLUG and TCR by 12 and 26 points. Where the model lacks the knowledge, the gains vanish, as the theory predicts.

items.title: A Heart Means Recursion: Exploring Visual Meaning and Communication in VLMs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A Heart Means Recursion: Exploring Visual Meaning and Communication in VLMs
items.summary: arXiv:2610.36449v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Do vision-language models (VLMs) share our ability to communicate visually? We share preliminary findings, starting from a surprising observation: simple visual symbols like a red heart can strongly influence model behavior on seemingly unrelated tasks, such as steering models towards recursive solutions on simple coding problems. Notably, this steering effect is largely implicit, as models' direct interpretations and thinking traces about visual symbols diverge substantially from their observed behavior. In visual communication between models, this leads to a generation--interpretation gap: while models tend to send shape primitives that they (and humans) find intuitive, these visual cues often fail to steer other models. In further communication games involving abstract concepts and stories, models can creatively use visuals to transmit meaning to one another, although some communications remain non-intuitive to humans. These findings reveal that VLMs might be capable of rich, creative, and visually-grounded communication, but their interpretation and production of visual meaning diverges from human conventions in surprising ways. Together this work highlights both the promise and challenges of visual communication between humans and VLMs.

items.title: AC-JEPA: Anchored Cross-Modal Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture for Visual-to-Symbolic Translation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AC-JEPA: Anchored Cross-Modal Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture for Visual-to-Symbolic Translation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.36493v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cross-modal translation requires models to capture shared semantics across modalities while preserving the fine-grained structure required by the target modality. Yet in real-world scientific domains, paired data are often imperfect, while obtaining clean pairs at scale is costly. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) directly optimizes cross-modal translation through categorical token-level supervision, but this objective is sensitive to errors in the target sequences. JEPA offers a complementary representation-space objective, but most existing formulations focus on prediction within a modality rather than translation across modalities. We introduce Anchored Cross-Modal JEPA (AC-JEPA), an SFT-compatible plug-in that predicts masked intermediate states in both cross-modal directions using paired data. The joint-embedding objective targets cross-modal structure predictable from context, while the causal SFT path retains direct token-level supervision for the target sequence. During self-training, AC-JEPA learns from continuous latent targets derived from imperfect pseudo-labeled pairs, offering intrinsic tolerance to local data errors without promoting pseudo-tokens to hard categorical supervision. Using optical chemical structure recognition as a testbed, AC-JEPA trained on clean pairs achieves 76.07% accuracy on the Simple set of the WildMol benchmark, compared with 67.40% for SFT alone. Using the same pseudo-labeled data for both approaches, AC-JEPA-based self-training further raises accuracy to 80.23%, whereas accuracy under direct SFT drops from 67.40% to 63.47%. These results support SFT-anchored joint-embedding prediction as an effective strategy for cross-modal translation under both curated and imperfect supervision.

items.title: MedConstBench: Benchmarking How Constitutions Steer LLMs in Medical Ethics [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: MedConstBench: Benchmarking How Constitutions Steer LLMs in Medical Ethics
items.summary: arXiv:2610.36513v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As large language models advance rapidly, they are increasingly used to answer medical questions, and many such models are now deployed locally. Once a model is deployed, its behavior is governed mainly by the ethical policy written into its constitution. However, most existing work focuses on factual correctness rather than the trade-off between competing ethical values. Even benchmarks that do evaluate ethics treat it as a fixed property of the model rather than as a variable, so how a constitution reshapes medical-ethics behavior remains largely unexplored. We introduce MedConstBench, a medical-ethics benchmark that treats the deployment constitution as a controlled variable, is organized around Beauchamp's four principles, and is scored by human-calibrated multi-model peer review. It includes MedDilemma, our own dataset of clinical dilemmas, and supports a systematic analysis of how constitutions steer LLMs. Evaluating ten open-source LLMs under four constitutions, we find that the effect of a constitution is dimension-selective and model-dependent, and that no constitution is universally optimal. Motivated by these findings, we propose a do-no-harm adaptive selector that chooses a constitution per model, matching the per-model oracle while guaranteeing a worst-case floor and generalizing to unseen models at low cost.

items.title: God Does Not Play Dice: Enforcing Batch Invariance in Agentic Kernel Generation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: God Does Not Play Dice: Enforcing Batch Invariance in Agentic Kernel Generation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.36623v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) serving systems dynamically batch user requests for GPU execution, so the same request may be processed alongside different requests across runs. If the GPU kernels lack batch invariance (BI), this changing batch context can alter the numerical output for an unchanged input, undermining reproducibility. Existing kernel generation agents focus on correctness and efficiency but \emph{overlook BI}. We find 19 confirmed BI violations among 83 batch-applicable released artifacts. To address this limitation, we propose \tool, which combines contract-guided static dependency analysis with dynamic validation of bitwise consistency across batch contexts. \tool is designed as a plug-in component for general kernel agents, allowing their original optimization capabilities to be reused while adding BI enforcement. We integrate it as successive acceptance gates in the optimization loop, rejecting structurally risky or dynamically non-invariant candidates before performance benchmarking and returning feedback to the agent. Experiments across three agent frameworks under baseline and BI-aware generation on real world LLM serving tasks show that \tool improves the BI pass rate from 67.6\% to 91.9\% while retaining 91.8\% of the baseline geometric mean speedup. These results demonstrate that \tool can be incorporated into kernel optimization by agents as an additional reliability objective alongside correctness and speed.

items.title: GUI-JEPA: Candidate-Conditioned JEPA Latents as a Fast Action Policy for Mobile GUI Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: GUI-JEPA: Candidate-Conditioned JEPA Latents as a Fast Action Policy for Mobile GUI Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2610.36877v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mobile GUI agents are typically fine-tuned 7B-scale vision-language models (VLMs) that generate each action as text. However, these VLMs decode every action token by token, and even agents that score candidate actions keep a large language model or VLM in the loop, making them slow and memory-hungry. To address these issues, we propose GUI-JEPA, to our knowledge the first decoder-free GUI agent policy built on a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA), which selects actions in the latent space of a JEPA encoder pretrained on unlabelled GUI screenshots. Its action- and region-conditioned latent predictor turns the screen latent into one latent per candidate action, letting lightweight heads score all candidates against the instruction in a single batched pass, without decoding a token. We further show that the scorer relies on this latent pathway and that the predictor is trained for the decision itself: a randomly initialised predictor does just as well as one pretrained on screen dynamics. On AndroidControl, GUI-JEPA is 2.8-4.0x faster on the same GPU than a Qwen2.5-VL-7B agent we fine-tune with the same inputs, while reaching 86-92% of its in-distribution accuracy with 6% of its parameters. Code is available at https://github.com/bcwang-sjtu/GUI-JEPA

items.title: RubricAtlas: Mining Type-Level Rubrics from Expert Reports to Evaluate Deep Research Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: RubricAtlas: Mining Type-Level Rubrics from Expert Reports to Evaluate Deep Research Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2610.36878v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep research agents conduct multi-step Web searches and synthesise retrieved information into analytical reports. Evaluating these outputs requires checking which analyses they deliver, beyond the presence of relevant facts. Query-specific binary rubrics make individual requirements explicit, but task-level checklists may leave the overall analytical structure underexamined. We introduce RubricAtlas, which derives type-level analytical requirements from expert reports on different objects within the same research type and organises detailed checks around recurring analytical questions. The requirements give related tasks a shared standard for what to analyse, without prescribing their answers. Our framework links binary checkpoints to report passages and evaluates completeness separately from argument validity. Built from 3,079 Chinese financial research reports, RubricAtlas covers 99 research types. Reference-report selection experiments show that individual reports cover only about half of their type's analytical questions, and that selecting requirements from different reports changes evaluation scores and agent rankings. Across ten agents, two judge pipelines achieve checkpoint agreement of $\kappa$ = 0.71 and agent-ranking agreement of Kendall $\tau$ = 0.87. Controlled deletions reduce scores on the affected analyses, while padding produces no detectable increase. These findings support type-level rubrics for comparing the analytical completeness of Web deep research outputs, with individual decisions traceable to report evidence.

items.title: AutoVend: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Long-Horizon Autonomous Vending Operations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AutoVend: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Long-Horizon Autonomous Vending Operations
items.summary: arXiv:2610.36980v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are extending agent-mediated commerce on the Web from shopping for consumers to operating businesses for sellers. In online-to-offline (O2O) commerce, decisions are issued through Web-based platforms but realized through costly physical execution. Evaluating such agents requires going beyond individual transactions to ask whether decisions made online turn into sustained economic returns. We introduce AutoVend, a benchmark in which one LLM agent manages 20 vending machines across five site types through a Web-based operating interface for 180 simulated days. Its data-grounded simulator combines a shared warehouse, procurement lead times, paid replenishment, inventory expiration, and recurring operating costs. We evaluate five LLM agents against a rule-based inventory-control baseline and diagnose their site coordination, execution, and performance over time. Four of five evaluated LLM agents fall short of this baseline, and returns per dollar of inference cost rank models differently from returns alone. Operational analyses show that gains in individual metrics do not consistently yield stronger economic growth, as inventory and execution costs erode these gains. Trajectory analysis further reveals difficulties in grounding feasible actions, managing inventory commitments, and converting feedback into effective policy revisions.
